questions.question: What does a `<View>` component actually compile down to on a real device?
options: An HTML <div> rendered in a hidden WebView
A real native view (UIView on iOS, ViewGroup on Android) — there is no DOM or browser involved
A JSON description that is never actually rendered natively
questions.explanation: React Native renders to genuine native platform views, not to HTML or a browser DOM — this is what distinguishes it from a web view wrapped in an app shell.

questions.question: What happens if you put a bare string directly inside a `<View>` without wrapping it in `<Text>`?
options: It renders exactly like it would on the web
React Native throws an error — unlike the web, text content must always be wrapped in a <Text> component
It silently renders as an empty View
It automatically gets wrapped in <Text> behind the scenes
questions.explanation: This is one of the first things that trips up developers coming from web React — React Native requires all text to be inside a <Text> element, with no silent auto-wrapping.

questions.question: Why does rendering a remote image with `<Image source={{ uri }} />` typically require explicit width/height styling?
options: React Native can't infer the image's dimensions from an unfetched remote resource the way a browser can for a loaded
Width and height are only needed for local images
It's purely a styling preference with no functional requirement
questions.explanation: Without a fetched image already in the layout pipeline, React Native has no dimensions to lay out with until you provide them explicitly.

questions.question: What is the key performance difference between `ScrollView` and `FlatList`?
options: There is no difference, they are aliases for the same component
ScrollView renders all of its children immediately; FlatList only renders items on or near screen and recycles rows as the user scrolls
ScrollView is the virtualized version and FlatList renders everything upfront
questions.explanation: FlatList's virtualization is what keeps long lists performant — ScrollView's render-everything-upfront behavior only works well for short, fixed content.
